paragraphs.where: Love doesn’t have to wait for trust, P5
paragraphs.before: When you're placing your younger self on trial, how valuable is it to consider how valuable it might have been for them to do what they did at the time, given what they knew at the time? How valuable is it to consider what options they had at the time and how tolerable they were? How valuable is it to consider what the consequences of their actions were at the time? How valuable is it to consider that, even though their actions at the time might have been harmful to you and others, punishing yourself now is not going to give them the capacity they needed at the time and that it's more useful to work on what you can do now to deal with the harm that was caused?
paragraphs.after: When you're placing your younger self on trial, instead of asking which age of you deserves the blame, ask: What was that age of you trying to get, or get away from? What did it understand back then? What options could it actually see? Could it stand to take any of them? What happened because of the choice it made? What was missing? Some ability, or help/protection from someone else? What can you learn or repair now, and how would you act differently in such situations? Even if what it did was harmful to you and others, punishing yourself now is not going to give it the capacity it needed at the time.

paragraphs.where: Finish without forcing a revelation, P1
paragraphs.before: Ending the session . Don’t feel that you have to end the session with a ‘great revelation’! When you have done as much as you want to do, it is a good idea to find out if there is anything that you need to do to make sure that you can leave things where they are for the time being. This might include thanking parts for their help, or making sure that you do something ‘in real life’ (eat a good meal, put a boundary in place, get some rest, repair a relationship, keep a promise etc) or it may be that there is nothing to do!
